page: UpCloud CLOUDNATIVE-6xCPU-16GB is a Cloud Native family virtual server running on the KVM hypervisor. It features 6 shared vCPUs mapped to 6 physical cores with 1.0 thread per core, utilizing an AMD EPYC 7542 processor clocked at 2.0 GHz. The system is equipped with 16.0 GB of RAM, providing 2.67 GB of memory per core. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware, but comes with one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark data reveals a split performance profile. The shared CPU allocation results in poor single-core CPU performance of 787.9 in stress-ng tests and weak multi-core performance of 4703.94. However, memory read bandwidth is average, reaching 616.67 GB/sec for small cached blocks and 43.56 GB/sec for large uncached blocks. Large block write bandwidth is weaker at 24.88 GB/sec. Geekbench scores are average, with a single-core score of 1351.0 and a multi-core score of 5544.0.

This server is suited for workloads that require moderate multi-threaded capabilities but do not demand sustained, dedicated CPU performance. Appropriate use cases include software compilation, text processing, and basic database operations, which scored in the average tier. It can handle light LLM inference on small models, but performance drops significantly on medium models. The shared CPU model offers a cost-efficient entry point for non-production environments, development testing, and general-purpose tasks where resource density is prioritized over dedicated compute guarantees.

This server does not include local storage or GPU accelerators. Performance benchmarks indicate a clear tradeoff: while single-core and multi-core raw CPU stress tests fall into the poor and weak categories due to the shared CPU allocation, memory read bandwidth and Geekbench multi-core processing remain average. The server handles software compilation, text processing, and small-model LLM inference adequately, but struggles with heavier compute tasks and medium-model text generation. It is best suited for development environments, lightweight database operations, and general-purpose workloads that benefit from a cost-efficient shared-resource model rather than dedicated, high-performance compute.
